documents.title: Syllabus Guidance Fall 2026 for UNH Durham and Manchester (section 1.5 Artificial Intelligence)
documents.summary: Provost syllabus guidance for Durham and Manchester. Its AI section urges explicit instructor expectations, prefers structured use over bans, supplies sample prohibit and permit statements, and sets rules for faculty use and detection tools.
documents.stance_why: The provost guidance sets no single rule: it says it is 'not to be prescriptive', recommends that instructors 'be very explicit', prefers guidance 'over blanket prohibition', and offers sample statements for a prohibited course and for a permitted course, so the decision goes to instructors.

units.why: The provost 'recommends that instructors be very explicit' about whether AI is allowed, which is a call to state AI expectations to students; P09 (state expectations in syllabus) fits, directed at instructors at course start.
units.anchor: recommends that instructors be very explicit with their students about whether any use of automated
units.policy: Instructors are recommended to be very explicit with students about whether any use of automated writing tools and AI tools is allowed and, if allowed, how and when.
units.fit_note: Recommends explicitness generally; does not strictly require a syllabus statement.

units.why: The university 'encourages guidance and support... over blanket prohibition', setting a default leaning toward structured permission; P02 is the nearest type though it is not a blanket permission.
units.anchor: encourages guidance and support in students’ use of generative AI over blanket prohibition
units.fit_note: Prefers guidance over blanket prohibition rather than stating AI is allowed by default.

units.why: The guidance cites 'Research on the prevalence of use and the impact' of AI on students as evidence for its stance, so it is a statement of evidence (P55) rather than a rule.
units.anchor: Research on the prevalence of use and the impact of generative AI use among college

units.why: States that 'pedagogically structured use... holds learning benefits'; this names benefits (and a risk) of AI for learning without a rule, so P87 and not P41 (which explains why a limit builds skill).
units.anchor: pedagogically structured use of generative AI holds learning benefits and unstructured use can harm learning
units.fit_note: Also says unstructured use can harm learning.

units.why: Says AI is 'embedded in professional and academic environments' and faculty must help students engage 'responsibly, ethically, and effectively'; teaching effective AI use as a professional skill fits P44.
units.anchor: faculty play a vital role in helping students develop the critical thinking skills
units.policy: As generative AI tools become increasingly embedded in professional and academic environments, faculty play a vital role in helping students develop the critical thinking skills needed to engage with these tools responsibly, ethically, and effectively.

units.why: Points faculty to 'Resources for designing assignments' on AI via a SharePoint site and teaching hub; this is faculty support in learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: Resources for designing assignments that promote authentic learning, intellectual ownership, and thoughtful AI engagement are

units.why: Offers an 'AI Assessment Scale' for instructors to disclose their course AI policy; a scale of levels of use is a tiered framework (P05), optional ('may also consider').
units.anchor: consider using this AI Assessment Scale as a basis for transparently disclosing your AI course

units.why: Recommends using the scale 'to start conversations with students about generative AI'; explaining and discussing the rules with students is P66, not P05, because the point is dialogue.
units.anchor: using this scale to start conversations with students about generative AI in your course

units.why: Sample syllabus text for instructors who choose a ban: generative AI 'is strictly prohibited in this course, even when properly attributed'; a default ban, P01, and it also says disclosure does not cure use.
units.anchor: is strictly prohibited in this course, even when properly attributed
units.policy: In the sample prohibition statement, the use of generative AI tools (e.g., Grammarly, ChatGPT, Claude AI, CoPilot) is strictly prohibited in the course, even when properly attributed.

units.why: Sample text classifies using generative AI to complete assignments as 'academic dishonesty' handled under existing policy, so it is P36 (misconduct classification).
units.anchor: is considered academic dishonesty (as defined by UNH’s Academic Integrity Policy)
units.policy: In the sample prohibition statement, using generative AI tools to complete assignments is considered academic dishonesty and is handled under existing policy.

units.why: Listed among things students are 'encouraged to' do under a ban: write using 'your own ideas and words', i.e. not have AI produce submitted text (P19); modality is should because the list is introduced as encouragement.
units.anchor: Complete all writing assignments using your own ideas and words.

units.why: Students are encouraged to keep 'version history' as evidence of their writing process; keeping drafts or logs that can be submitted is P26.
units.anchor: Turn on version history in Microsoft Word to demonstrate your iterative writing process.

units.why: Students should 'be prepared to describe your work and the process', meaning they must be able to explain what they submitted (P30).
units.anchor: Be prepared to describe your work and the process you used.

units.why: Tells students to 'Ask the course instructor' when unsure what is acceptable, exactly P10.
units.anchor: Ask the course instructor if you’re unsure whether a tool or method is acceptable

units.why: Sample text prohibits 'Using AI to transcribe or summarize course lectures' unless SAS approves; P86 covers AI transcription of class sessions, though here it is a ban with an SAS exception rather than a consent rule.
units.anchor: Using AI to transcribe or summarize course lectures.
units.fit_note: A ban on AI transcription or summarization of lectures with an SAS-approval exception, not a consent-before-recording rule.

units.why: Sample text lists 'Uploading instructor-created course materials to an AI tool' as prohibited, matching P49.
units.anchor: Uploading instructor-created course materials to an AI tool for the purposes of summary generation.

units.why: Makes SAS approval the route by which otherwise prohibited AI uses become allowed, i.e. AI as an accessibility accommodation (P97); it is also a restrictive clause, so the fit is partial.
units.anchor: unless specifically approved by Student Accessibility Services (SAS), other uses of AI are prohibited
units.fit_note: Frames SAS approval as the only exception to the list of prohibited AI uses; does not describe accessible AI output or reviews.

units.why: The sample ban is justified because it 'supports your independent development of reading comprehension, content creation, and writing', i.e. doing the work builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: supports your independent development of reading comprehension, content creation, and writing

units.why: The sample permissive statement 'supports the use of generative AI as a tool', a default allowing AI (P02).
units.anchor: supports the use of generative AI as a tool
units.policy: In the sample permissive statement, the course policy supports the use of generative AI as a tool.

units.why: Adds that AI is 'not a replacement for your own thinking and learning', so the student stays the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: not a replacement for your own thinking and learning
units.policy: In the sample permissive statement, generative AI is a tool and not a replacement for the student's own thinking and learning.

units.why: Says AI may 'extend your thinking' and 'help with supplementary tasks' so students can focus on analysis, a statement of benefits (P87) rather than a rule.
units.anchor: extend your thinking in valuable ways and (2) help with supplementary tasks

units.why: Because AI 'can produce inaccurate responses', students are 'expected to critically evaluate and cross-verify' output; this is verification of AI output (P31), with responsibility for accuracy as a related point.
units.anchor: expected to critically evaluate and cross-verify information produced by AI tools

units.why: States that 'Specific assignments may permit or require' AI, so the rule is set per assignment (P04); the 'require' part would be P79 but the sentence mainly says assignments decide.
units.anchor: Specific assignments may permit or require the use of generative AI tools.
units.fit_note: Also says some assignments may require AI use (P79).

units.why: Students must read each assignment's own instructions to learn what AI use is allowed, matching P78 (learn and follow each course's rules).
units.anchor: pay close attention to individual assignment instructions

units.why: Where tools are permitted, they 'should be used only in the manner specified' and with 'proper citation to the tool'. The citation requirement is the clearest rule (P24); the 'manner specified' limit goes with it.
units.anchor: they should be used only in the manner specified, and with caution and proper citation
units.policy: If automated writing tools are permitted for an assignment, they should be used only in the manner specified, and with caution and proper citation to the tool.
units.fit_note: Combines citation with a duty to use the tool only as the assignment specifies.

units.why: Tells students 'do not share sensitive, protected, or restricted data' with AI tools because tools store prompts; data protection is P50.
units.anchor: do not share sensitive, protected, or restricted data as this may violate privacy or intellectual

units.why: When unsure whether data may go into AI, 'ask your faculty member or do not use AI tools'; this is ask-before-use (P10).
units.anchor: When in doubt, ask your faculty member or do not use AI tools on such

units.why: Says AI-detection software is 'unreliable' and 'biased', which is the reason not to rely on detectors (P39).
units.anchor: These tools are unreliable and have been shown to be biased against certain segments of

units.why: Detector output 'should not be used to make definitive judgments' on integrity, i.e. at most supporting evidence, which the broadened P69 covers; P39 fits less because it concerns unreliability, not the evidence standard.
units.anchor: should not be used to make definitive judgments about academic integrity

units.why: Warns that detectors 'may incorrectly flag accessibility tools', a specific reason detectors are unreliable (P39).
units.anchor: AI detection tools also may incorrectly flag accessibility tools
units.fit_note: Specifically about false flags on accessibility tools.

units.why: Faculty 'should discuss the use of accessibility tools' in advance with SAS-approved students, an accessibility rule (P97).
units.anchor: Faculty should discuss the use of accessibility tools with students who have been approved by

units.why: Student work 'should not be uploaded to any third-party tool' unless USNH approved; protecting data and using vetted tools is P50.
units.anchor: should not be uploaded to any third-party tool, including AI detection platforms, unless that tool
units.policy: Student work should not be uploaded to any third-party tool, including AI detection platforms, unless USNH has explicitly approved the tool for sharing student work.

units.why: Says uploading identifiable student documents 'constitutes a violation of FERPA', tying AI use to existing law (P77).
units.anchor: constitutes a violation of FERPA
units.policy: Uploading documents that contain student names, emails, or ID numbers, or are otherwise identifiable, constitutes a violation of FERPA.

units.why: Says de-identification 'alone does not make uploading... permissible' because student work may carry IP protection (P52).
units.anchor: de-identification alone does not make uploading that work to third-party tools permissible

units.why: Faculty 'are required to consult the approved tools list' before reviewing student work with a tool, a rule to use approved tools (P92).
units.anchor: faculty are required to consult the approved tools list and confirm the appropriate data tier

units.why: Faculty are encouraged to read guidance 'on discussing expectations with students', i.e. explaining and discussing AI rules (P66).
units.anchor: guidance on discussing expectations with students
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to review the Academic Honesty and AI Policy: Transparency, Consistency and Student Conversations for guidance on discussing expectations with students.

units.why: AI-assisted evaluation of student work is allowed only with USNH-approved tools, a condition on AI-assisted grading (P101).
units.anchor: Only USNH approved tools (such as DeepThought and Enterprise-level CoPilot through SSO) may be used

units.why: Faculty 'must disclose' their AI use to students, P47.
units.anchor: You must disclose your use of AI-enabled tools to students

units.why: Faculty must make clear that 'AI will not replace your own evaluation of work', so a human does the evaluating (P46).
units.anchor: AI will not replace your own evaluation of work

units.why: Instructors who restrict students are 'expected to model the same standards of transparency', a commitment on instructor AI use mirrored to students (P47).
units.anchor: expected to model the same standards of transparency and responsible use they require of their
units.fit_note: A modeling expectation that faculty meet the standards they set students, not only disclosure.

units.why: 'departments are encouraged to establish shared norms around faculty AI use' lets units set their own faculty-use rules (P85).
units.anchor: departments are encouraged to establish shared norms around faculty AI use
units.fit_note: Concerns department-level norms for faculty use, not student rules.

units.why: Faculty 'are required to get explicit approval from ET&S' before sharing student work with non-USNH tools, an institutional approval of tools and data sharing (P65).
units.anchor: faculty are required to get explicit approval from ET&S to share student work for that

units.why: Sample syllabus statement in which the instructor discloses that they 'may use USNH approved' AI tools to assess de-identified work: instructor disclosure to students (P47).
units.anchor: I may use USNH approved artificial intelligence-enabled tools

units.why: The sample statement commits that 'Any findings from AI tools will be reviewed by me', human review of AI-assisted grading (P101).
units.anchor: Any findings from AI tools will be reviewed by me

units.why: The sample statement says tool use 'adheres to university policies' and FERPA, i.e. AI use complies with existing policy and law (P77).
units.anchor: adheres to university policies on academic integrity, the protection of student data (FERPA)

units.why: Students may 'request that your work be reviewed... without AI assistance' and this 'must be honored', an opt-out alternative; nearest type is P51 (alternatives exist), though it is about grading, not tool access.
units.anchor: you have the right to request that your work be reviewed by me without AI
units.fit_note: An opt-out of AI-assisted grading, not about cost or access to AI tools.

units.why: The student-conduct definition of plagiarism, copied from the SRRR, includes 'computer generated text', so AI-generated text submitted uncited is misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: including computer generated text or work outsourced to third parties

units.why: The definition of cheating lists 'AI tools' used 'without authorization', classifying unauthorized AI use as cheating (P36).
units.anchor: electronic data, AI tools, assignment/exam surrogate, or other forms of assistance without authorization

units.why: Describes who contributed to the guidance document (which includes the AI section), matching P84 (how and by whom the guidance was made).
units.anchor: culmination of input from multiple faculty committees, multiple senate committees, student support offices
units.fit_note: Describes the whole syllabus guidance, not only the AI section.

documents.title: Graduate Catalog: Academic Integrity (Guidance on Permissibility of Generative AI Use in Graduate Exams and Theses)
documents.summary: Graduate Catalog guidance on generative AI in graduate exams and theses. It leaves the permission decision to programs, requires disclosure and committee authorization of any use, and treats unapproved use as misconduct.
documents.stance_why: The Graduate School says it 'does not have a universal policy' and that programs 'may prohibit' or 'may allow' generative AI in exams and theses, so each program decides, while it sets disclosure and approval conditions.

units.why: The Graduate School says it 'does not have a universal policy', leaving the rule to programs; P85 (units set their own rules).
units.anchor: the Graduate School does not have a universal policy regarding the permissibility of using generative

units.why: Programs 'should explicitly communicate' their AI expectations to students, P09 (state expectations), directed at programs.
units.anchor: Programs should explicitly communicate to students their expectations for whether and how generative AI may

units.why: Specifies timing: expectations are 'conveyed in writing when students first matriculate and again before their exams', a communication rule (P09).
units.anchor: conveyed in writing when students first matriculate and again before their exams and theses/dissertations
units.fit_note: Adds timing (at matriculation and before exams/theses) to the communication duty.

units.why: Programs 'may prohibit' AI for graduate exams and theses while 'others may allow it', so each program sets its own rule (P85).
units.anchor: Some programs may prohibit the use of generative AI for these purposes

units.why: Programs should keep handbooks and orientation materials current as they set expectations, a duty to update policy (P54), partial since it is about documents rather than review cycles.
units.anchor: updating relevant handbooks, orientation materials, and mentor guidelines
units.fit_note: Updating handbooks, orientation materials and mentor guidelines; no review cycle or feedback invited.

units.why: Students 'must disclose' use with 'what tool(s)... how, and when'; the specified details make this P25 rather than the general P24.
units.anchor: must disclose such use, including an explanation of what tool(s) were used, how, and when

units.why: AI uses in exams and theses 'must be communicated to, and authorized by, the advisor and... committee'; this is a rule for research and scholarship (P62).
units.anchor: must be communicated to, and authorized by, the advisor and relevant academic committee
units.fit_note: Requires advisor and committee authorization of each AI use.

units.why: Graduate exams and theses 'must represent the student's own scholarly work': students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: must represent the student’s own scholarly work

units.why: AI 'may be used for approved and clearly acknowledged purposes' with committee approval; this is graduate-thesis AI governance (P62), permissive only under approval.
units.anchor: AI tools may be used for approved and clearly acknowledged purposes upon receiving the necessary

units.why: 'the intellectual contributions must be the student's own' keeps the student the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: the intellectual contributions must be the student’s own

units.why: 'Any use of AI tools must be properly cited' is a citation duty (P24).
units.anchor: Any use of AI tools must be properly cited according to disciplinary norms.

units.why: 'Unapproved use... constitutes academic misconduct', classifying misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Unapproved use of generative AI in exams, theses, or dissertations constitutes academic misconduct

units.why: States the penalty in advance: 'grounds for failure of the relevant exam or thesis' (P37).
units.anchor: is grounds for failure of the relevant exam or thesis

units.why: Directs reporting and appeals to the formal Academic Integrity procedure, matching P81.
units.anchor: The reporting and appeals process for all academic misconduct should follow the Academic Integrity policy

documents.title: USNH Guidelines for the Use and Procurement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools
documents.summary: System-level IT guidelines on using and buying generative AI tools. They cover data protection, accountability for AI content, phishing, and security review before procurement, and refer academic integrity to local policy.
documents.stance_why: The guidelines say USNH 'supports the responsible exploration of these tools' and set conditions (protect data, be accountable, check output), without banning use or delegating the decision wholesale; academic-integrity rules are referred to each institution.

units.why: The system 'supports the responsible exploration of these tools', a default welcoming AI use with conditions (P02).
units.anchor: USNH supports the responsible exploration of these tools

units.why: Says the guidelines 'build on existing USNH policies', so AI use falls under existing rules (P77).
units.anchor: These guidelines build on existing USNH policies rather than introducing new requirements.

units.why: The system will 'monitor advancements, gather feedback... and update these guidelines', a commitment to revisit (P54).
units.anchor: continue to monitor advancements, gather feedback from the university community, and update these guidelines

units.why: 'Do not input data classified as confidential or sensitive' into public AI tools is a data-protection rule (P50) binding all users.
units.anchor: Do not input data classified as confidential or sensitive (Tier 2 and above) into publicly

units.why: Explains that data shared with AI tools 'may not be private', the reason for protecting data (P50).
units.anchor: Information shared with AI tools using default settings may not be private

units.why: 'Users are accountable for any content' with AI-generated material, so users own what they publish (P29).
units.anchor: Users are accountable for any content they produce or publish that incorporates AI-generated material.

units.why: Warns that AI content 'may be inaccurate, misleading, or fabricated', the premise for verifying output (P31).
units.anchor: AI-generated content may be inaccurate, misleading, or fabricated

units.why: AI content 'could contain copyrighted material', a copyright concern (P52).
units.anchor: could contain copyrighted material

units.why: 'should be carefully reviewed for accuracy and compliance' is a verification duty (P31).
units.anchor: All AI-generated content should be carefully reviewed for accuracy and compliance before dissemination.

units.why: Tells users to 'Refer to your institution's... handbooks' for integrity policy, i.e. to look up the rules that apply (P78).
units.anchor: Refer to your institution’s student and faculty handbooks for policies on academic integrity.

units.why: Lets each institution or department update its own policies, so units set their own rules (P85).
units.anchor: Each USNH institution or department may update its policies

units.why: Faculty are 'encouraged to clearly communicate permitted uses of AI', a call to state expectations (P09).
units.anchor: encouraged to clearly communicate permitted uses of AI in coursework and academic activities

units.why: Students 'should proactively seek clarification from instructors', i.e. ask when unsure (P10).
units.anchor: Students should proactively seek clarification from instructors when necessary.

units.why: Under 'Be Vigilant Against AI-Enabled Phishing', users should 'report any suspicious communications'; AI phishing awareness (P75).
units.anchor: report any suspicious communications to ET&S Client Services

units.why: Before acquiring AI tools users should consult ET&S or request a security review, institutional tool approval (P65).
units.anchor: consult with ET&S about options to fit your needs or request a Security Assessment Review

units.why: 'must undergo a risk assessment... before use' is review of AI tools before deployment (P65).
units.anchor: Any vendor-provided AI tools must undergo a risk assessment by the USNH Cybersecurity team before

notes: Computing, school and course layers none-found or deferred in the collect file; only university-layer documents coded. Several units use fit_note where a type fits partly (P97 for the SAS exception, P86 for the AI-transcription ban, P02 for the 'guidance over prohibition' preference).
